subject: english-language
title: Naming the Genre
welcome_lead: Spot the genre by its tell-tale signs.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on identifying fiction genres.
final_note: You can now name the genre from setting and plot clues.

concepts.def: Event type that hints at genre.

walkthroughs.body_html: Dragons hint fantasy; spaceships hint sci-fi; a body in a library hints mystery. Conventions are the signs.
Genre also links to audience and purpose. A horror story aims to scare adult readers; a fairy tale aims to teach children.
Combine setting clues (where/when) and plot clues (what happens) to confirm a genre quickly.

mcqs.q: An expected feature of a genre is a.
Why a text was written is its.
Why do text types have predictable features?
options: Conventions develop because they serve communicative purpose — a recipe needs imperatives because it instructs; a news report needs the inverted pyramid because of how readers scan.
Text types have fixed features just because tradition says so.
Inflectional morphology applies only to verbs and derivational only to nouns.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between inflectional and derivational morphology?
options: Inflectional morphology applies only to verbs and derivational only to nouns.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.

Inflectional morphemes mark grammatical features without changing word class (cat/cats, walk/walked); derivational morphemes create new words, often changing word class (happy → happiness, teach → teacher).
Inflection and derivation are two words for the same process.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a dialect and an accent?
options: A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
Text types are arbitrary and have no patterns.
Dialect and accent mean the same thing.
Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation — so all dialects involve accents but not vice versa.
